1w Your migration can turn a paying subscriber into a decline. For a recurring payment to work, the network needs to recognize its link to the customer’s original consent. Those identifiers often live inside the current payment setup. Move processors without preserving that chain and an established subscriber can look like a first-time payer. The card has not necessarily changed. The proof that it belongs to a valid recurring agreement may be missing. Network tokens have their own relationship and onboarding dependencies. 1w The clock for a review request starts at the door. A checkout date tells you when money changed hands. It does not tell you whether a customer has received the product, let alone experienced it. When a review request fires while the parcel is still in transit, you are not collecting product feedback. You are inviting delivery frustration into a retention moment. Use two conditions: → confirmed delivery → enough time to use the product The second condition changes by category. For many physical goods, 7 to 14 days after confirmed delivery is a reasonable starting point. Then stop the sequence once the customer responds. Trigger off the event. Not the schedule. 2w A customer pays. Their card is charged. But the order never reaches fulfillment. No pick ticket. No shipment. Then the support ticket arrives, and someone has to rebuild the order or issue a refund. This is rarely a warehouse problem. It is usually a blast-radius problem. When multiple stores share one account-level webhook endpoint and event scope, a configuration change for one store can interrupt order events for all of them. The better pattern is store-level isolation: • one endpoint per store • one event scope per store • one clear owner per store
